prompt.brief: Design a reliable on-call scheduling and escalation service that resolves current ownership across rotations, sends multi-channel alerts, escalates on timeout, and preserves an auditable incident timeline.
successSignals: Define schedules, rotations, overrides, time zones, holidays, teams, escalation policies, incident acknowledgments, and notification attempts.
Resolve one deterministic responder for a point in time, handle handoffs and concurrent edits, and never silently drop an urgent alert.
Separate schedule reads from alert intake, delivery workers, provider callbacks, audit history, and escalation timers; make retries idempotent.
Explain provider outage, quiet hours, deduplication, privacy, access controls, observability, and emergency fallback contacts.

functional: Create teams/schedules, define rotations and overrides, resolve current on-call ownership, ingest incidents, and send/escalate notifications.
Support acknowledgment, snooze, handoff, maintenance windows, multi-channel delivery, delivery receipts, and escalation timelines.
Make schedule changes versioned, retries deduplicated, contacts auditable, personal data controlled, and missed notifications recoverable.
nonFunctional: Resolve ownership immediately and deliver or escalate critical alerts within the configured policy window with visible delivery state.
Handle 100k incidents per day and large notification bursts without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Reliable on-call scheduling commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Reliable on-call scheduling writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Reliable on-call scheduling version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Reliable on-call scheduling by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Reliable on-call scheduling work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Reliable on-call scheduling projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Reliable on-call scheduling projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Reliable on-call scheduling records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Reliable on-call scheduling latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
